question: Which way of moving drugs across cell membranes needs the body to spend actual energy (ATP)?

options.A: Passive diffusion
options.B: Facilitated diffusion
options.C: Simple filtration
options.D: Active transport

explanation: Just like climbing a hill requires energy, 'active' transport uses cellular energy to pump substances across membranes, often against a flow.

question: Why do nurse researchers read past studies before starting a new project?

options.A: To guarantee that the new study will cost no money
options.B: To ensure that all previous researchers were entirely wrong
options.C: To bypass the need for any formal hospital ethical approval
options.D: To avoid repeating work that has already been done

explanation: Checking existing studies saves you time and resources so you don't reinvent the wheel on questions already answered.

question: What are the two primary organs that make up the central nervous system?

options.A: Nerves and ganglia
options.B: Spinal cord and peripheral nerves
options.C: Brain and spinal cord
options.D: Cerebrum and cerebellum

explanation: The central nervous system is strictly composed of the brain and the spinal cord, separating it from the peripheral nervous system. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T3#GNS211_U3_T3_h1)

question: Which Nigerian agency is well-known for child protection and rescuing minors from trafficking and abuse?

options.A: Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation
options.B: Central Bank of Nigeria
options.C: NAPTIP
options.D: Federal Road Safety Corps

explanation: NAPTIP (National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons) is at the forefront of protecting Nigerian children from abuse and exploitation.

question: What is the main thing that separates a true experiment from a quasi-experiment?

options.A: Avoiding all forms of statistical testing
options.B: The use of patient interviews for data collection
options.C: The presence of a clinical nurse researcher
options.D: Random assignment of participants to groups

explanation: You nailed it! True experiments use random chance (like flipping a coin) to drop people into different groups, while quasi-experiments don't use strict random mixing. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T13#GNS217_U3_T13_h4)

question: Which cooking method is best to suggest for reducing dietary fat intake?

options.A: Deep frying in lard
options.B: Pan frying in butter
options.C: Baking or steaming
options.D: Sautéeing in heavy oil

explanation: Baking and steaming let you cook delicious meals without pouring in extra oils, butter, or animal fats.

question: Why is having 'zero complaints' from nurses NOT always a sign that a hospital software program is working well?

options.A: Nurses may have given up or created workarounds instead of reporting issues
options.B: Hospital computers block all feedback messages sent by staff
options.C: Software automatically fixes its own design errors over time
options.D: Nurses prefer spending extra hours clicking through bad menus

explanation: So true! When systems are frustrating, busy nurses often just find quiet workarounds instead of wasting time filing formal complaints.

question: What test is commonly used to check if a patient is strong enough to come off mechanical ventilation?

options.A: Arterial blood gas challenge
options.B: Continuous positive pressure test
options.C: Pulmonary function spirometry
options.D: Spontaneous breathing trial

explanation: A spontaneous breathing trial lets the patient test-drive their own lungs with very little machine help for a short period to see if they are ready to breathe entirely on their own.

question: What is the main reason for holding community disaster drills?

options.A: To replace the need for written emergency preparedness guides
options.B: To help residents turn emergency knowledge into practical muscle memory
options.C: To punish people who fail to follow local sanitation laws
options.D: To test the physical strength of professional rescue workers

explanation: You're doing great! Drills give people practice so they can react quickly and calmly when a real emergency strikes.

question: How do learning disabilities differ from global developmental delays?

options.A: Learning disabilities impact every single area of daily physical and mental functioning
options.B: Global delays only appear during adulthood while learning disabilities appear in infancy
options.C: Learning disabilities affect specific academic areas while overall intelligence remains intact
options.D: Global delays are caused exclusively by environmental factors rather than brain function

explanation: Specific learning challenges target isolated skills like reading or math, unlike global delays that affect all areas of development. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T6#GNS324_U4_T6_h1)

question: What is the main goal of community programs that prevent child abuse?

options.A: Removing all children from high-risk neighborhoods
options.B: Strengthening families and reducing stress before crises occur
options.C: Punishing parents who fail to attend community meetings
options.D: Replacing social welfare agencies with nurse-led clinics

explanation: Good prevention programs give parents the tools, coping skills, and support they need before things ever reach a crisis point.

question: You want to start an immunization campaign in a rural town. What should be your very first step?

options.A: Consult with local leaders and respect community values
options.B: Import expensive foreign medications without checking needs
options.C: Call the police to force every parent to bring their child
options.D: Build a brand-new private hospital without telling residents

explanation: Spot on! Working hand-in-hand with local leaders builds immediate trust and ensures the community happily joins in to protect their health.

question: What is the main reason we use the ABCDEF protocol in emergency care?

options.A: To document nursing care for legal cover
options.B: To figure out the final medical diagnosis
options.C: To replace the need for lab tests
options.D: To find and treat life-threatening problems step-by-step

explanation: You've got this! The ABCDEF guide helps healthcare teams tackle the scariest, most immediate life threats first so nothing gets missed. Great job thinking like an emergency nurse!

question: What happens during an 'ascending infection' in the female reproductive system?

options.A: Pathogens move upward from the vagina and cervix into the uterus and fallopian tubes
options.B: Viruses migrate from skin lesions down to the regional lymph nodes
options.C: Fungi multiply rapidly on the external vulva and travel to the bladder
options.D: Bacteria travel through the bloodstream directly to the heart valves

explanation: An ascending infection is just germs traveling upward—moving past the cervix and into the upper reproductive organs where they can cause serious trouble.

question: A family member asks how to wash bed sheets stained with wound drainage. What should you tell them?

options.A: Wash the linens separately using hot water and standard detergent
options.B: Soak the linens in cold outdoor water before throwing them away
options.C: Wash the soiled sheets together with the family's weekly clothing
options.D: Hang the sheets in the sun without washing to kill the bacteria

explanation: Hot water and separate washing are key here! It breaks down the mess and stops germs from spreading to the rest of the household laundry.

question: Which of the following is a primary example of consumer health informatics?

options.A: University nursing curriculum accreditation databases
options.B: Internal staff attendance registers used by nurse managers
options.C: Patient portals and wearable fitness tracking applications
options.D: Hospital financial ledger and budgeting software programs

explanation: Consumer health informatics centers on tools that patients use directly to track and manage their personal health. [learn more](GNS113_U1_T2#GNS113_U1_T2_h6)

question: How do oxygen and carbon dioxide move across the alveolar-capillary membrane?

options.A: Active transport
options.B: Simple diffusion
options.C: Pinocytosis
options.D: Osmotic pressure

explanation: Gases move naturally across the thin membrane from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration without using cellular energy. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T9#GNS111_U2_T9_h4)

question: Why are standard gravity IV drips unreliable in a moving ambulance?

options.A: Changing road angles and vehicle motion alter the fluid flow rate
options.B: Plastic IV bags automatically dissolve when exposed to engine exhaust
options.C: The vibration makes the fluid change its chemical composition
options.D: Nurses are legally forbidden from using bags inside vehicles

explanation: As the ambulance accelerates, brakes, and turns corners, the angle of the fluid relative to the patient shifts, making infusion pumps much safer. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T9#GNS315_U3_T9_h5)

question: Why must you check if two drugs are compatible before adding an IV piggyback medicine into an existing line?

options.A: Hospital pharmacy software blocks incompatible infusions anyway.
options.B: Primary fluids neutralize the therapeutic effect of all antibiotics.
options.C: Incompatible drugs can form precipitates that block the catheter.
options.D: Mismatched drugs will automatically cause severe patient hypertension.

explanation: Spot on! Mixing the wrong drugs can cause chemical reactions that turn into solid gunk, clogging the line and endangering the patient.

question: Why is integrating basic mental health services into primary healthcare clinics an effective strategy?

options.A: It stops patients from ever needing medication in the future
options.B: It guarantees that patients will never experience stress again
options.C: It makes mental health care more accessible and reduces social stigma
options.D: It eliminates the need for any nurses or doctors to be present

explanation: When mental health care is offered right inside regular primary clinics, patients can seek help easily without the shame of visiting a specialized psychiatric hospital. [learn more](GNS314_U1_T7#GNS314_U1_T7_h8)

question: In nursing research, what does 'validity' simply mean?

options.A: How truly a study measures what it claims to measure
options.B: How fast a computer can run the data
options.C: Whether the paper was published in a big journal
options.D: How many patients took part in the study

explanation: Think of validity as truthfulness! It just checks if the research tool or study is actually measuring what it says it is measuring.

question: Which of the following is NOT a helpful way to support someone through quarantine?

options.A: Helping them stay connected using digital tools
options.B: Ignoring their emotional complaints to save time
options.C: Ensuring access to food and medicine supplies
options.D: Providing clear education on symptom monitoring

explanation: Ignoring emotional distress increases anxiety and can cause individuals to break quarantine out of frustration. [learn more](GST114_U2_T16#GST114_U2_T16_h6)

question: Why must reusable tools like ultrasound probes be carefully disinfected after every single patient?

options.A: To prevent the spread of hospital-acquired infections
options.B: To make the machine look brand new to the patient
options.C: To improve the clarity of the computer images
options.D: To ensure the battery stays fully charged

explanation: Wiping down equipment stops germs from hitching a ride from one patient to the next. You're building great clinical habits!

question: Which of these is NOT a common reason why infectious diseases end up underreported in clinics?

options.A: Ignorance of the list of notifiable diseases
options.B: Fear of blame or administrative punishment by management
options.C: Excessive availability of rapid diagnostic testing kits
options.D: Heavy clinical workloads and lack of reporting forms

explanation: Great job! Having plenty of testing kits would actually make reporting easier, not harder. Heavy workloads and fear are the real culprits behind underreporting.

question: Why is putting way too many overlapping lines on a single graph a bad idea?

options.A: It violates international laws regarding hospital record keeping.
options.B: It prevents the horizontal axis from showing future time intervals.
options.C: It creates an unreadable tangle of ink that defeats the purpose of a visual aid.
options.D: It automatically changes the numerical values of the raw data.

explanation: Exactly! Graphs are supposed to make data clear and simple. Too many lines just create a messy web that is impossible to read.

question: Why do doctors most commonly perform a colostomy?

options.A: To permanently cure long-term constipation without changing diet
options.B: To bypass or remove a diseased or damaged part of the bowel
options.C: To allow direct medicine administration into the bloodstream
options.D: To increase the length of the small intestine for better food absorption

explanation: Spot on! Conditions like severe infection, injury, or cancer mean we need to safely divert waste away from a sick section of the large intestine.

question: Which phase of disaster management involves running community drills and stocking up on emergency supplies?

options.A: Recovery
options.B: Preparedness
options.C: Response
options.D: Mitigation

explanation: Well done! Preparedness means taking proactive steps beforehand so our systems and teams are ready when trouble strikes.

question: What is the main job of your eustachian tube when you yawn or swallow on a flight?

options.A: To amplify high-frequency sound waves
options.B: To translate fluid waves into nerve impulses
options.C: To equalize air pressure in the middle ear
options.D: To produce earwax for protection

explanation: That "pop" you feel in your ears when swallowing helps the eustachian tube let air in or out, keeping the pressure balanced on both sides of your eardrum.

question: Which of the following is NOT a common reason for excluding a child from a nursery temporarily?

options.A: Persistent vomiting or unexplained severe diarrhea
options.B: A mild, clear runny nose without any fever or lethargy
options.C: An undiagnosed, contagious vesicular skin rash
options.D: A high fever accompanied by unusual lethargy

explanation: Mild upper respiratory symptoms like a clear runny nose without fever do not typically require exclusion, whereas contagious rashes, vomiting, and high fevers do. [learn more](GNS225_U4_T8#GNS225_U4_T8_h5)

question: Which single cranial nerve carries most of the parasympathetic signals to the chest and tummy organs?

options.A: Optic nerve
options.B: Vagus nerve
options.C: Hypoglossal nerve
options.D: Trigeminal nerve

explanation: The vagus nerve (Cranial Nerve X) is the main highway for parasympathetic signals, carrying about three-quarters of all outgoing signals to your internal organs. Excellent recall!

question: What is the main virus that causes COVID-19?

options.A: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
options.B: SARS-CoV-2
options.C: Influenza A virus
options.D: Respiratory Syncytial Virus

explanation: COVID-19 stands for coronavirus disease 2019, and it is caused by the specific virus called Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). You've got this! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h1)

question: How does MBO directly improve day-to-day nursing workflows?

options.A: By eliminating all paperwork required during patient handovers
options.B: By allowing nurses to prescribe medications independently
options.C: By ensuring nurses never have to work night shifts again
options.D: By giving nurses clear performance targets that reduce confusion

explanation: Clear objectives remove ambiguity, helping nurses prioritize critical clinical tasks during chaotic shifts. [learn more](GST321_U2_T5#GST321_U2_T5_h5)

question: Which cranial nerve is mainly responsible for controlling the muscles of the oesophagus?

options.A: Glossopharyngeal nerve
options.B: Hypoglossal nerve
options.C: Trigeminal nerve
options.D: Vagus nerve

explanation: Correct! The vagus nerve is the major highway for signals that coordinate those smooth swallowing contractions.

question: How long should a food handler scrub their hands with soap and water?

options.A: As long as 5 minutes
options.B: Up to 2 minutes
options.C: Exactly 5 seconds
options.D: At least 20 seconds

explanation: Scrubbing with soap for a minimum of 20 seconds is the magic number to properly wash away germs on the skin. You're doing great!

question: As a nurse, what is a key care step for a patient being treated for polycythaemia?

options.A: Giving high-dose iron with meals
options.B: Restricting all physical movement to bed rest
options.C: Applying warm compresses to the legs
options.D: Encouraging plenty of fluids to stop sluggish blood

explanation: Fluid is key! Drinking enough water keeps the thick blood moving smoothly and prevents dangerous clots.

question: Why does severe peripheral vascular disease often lead to an amputation?

options.A: Blocked arteries prevent oxygen and nutrients from reaching tissues, causing cell death.
options.B: High blood pressure forces the limb to swell until the skin splits open.
options.C: Excess fluid builds up in the muscles and causes the bone to snap.
options.D: Weakened veins allow blood to pool and turn into dangerous blood clots.

explanation: Think of it like a plant without water—when blood flow is cut off, the tissue lacks oxygen and dies, which can create gangrene that requires surgery. Great job learning the basics!

question: Which of the following is a major risk when electronic health record systems experience sudden downtime?

options.A: All medication pumps stop working simultaneously
options.B: Staff must revert to paper charting, which can increase transcription errors
options.C: Hospital doors automatically lock to prevent patient entry
options.D: Patient vital signs automatically delete themselves from memory

explanation: System downtime forces a return to manual paper records, raising the chance of mistakes during handovers and order transcription. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T4#GNS113_U2_T4_h7)

question: You check a patient's blood pressure and find it dangerously high while they complain of severe chest pain. What do you do right away?

options.A: Erase the reading and take it again tomorrow
options.B: Wait until the shift handover meeting later that evening
options.C: Leave the patient room without telling anyone
options.D: Report the critical findings verbally to the physician immediately

explanation: Critical changes need fast action! Always speak up and report urgent findings right away to senior staff or the doctor so the patient gets help immediately.

question: How does the body's immune system play a role in letting endometriosis develop?

options.A: It causes an overproduction of red blood cells during menses
options.B: It produces antibodies that destroy normal uterine muscle tissue
options.C: It fails to clear misplaced endometrial cells from the pelvic cavity
options.D: It permanently blocks the normal release of estrogen and progesterone

explanation: Normally, our immune system cleans up stray cells. In endometriosis, the local immune defense drops the ball, allowing those stray cells to stick around and grow.

question: At what age might a nurse suspect a motor issue if an infant consistently prefers using only one hand?

options.A: By one month of age
options.B: Only during school age
options.C: Before eighteen months
options.D: Around three years old

explanation: Babies usually don't show a strong hand preference early on. Showing one-sided preference before 18 months can be an early sign of hemiplegic cerebral palsy.

question: What is the main danger if a third-degree tear is missed and left unrepaired after childbirth?

options.A: Delayed involution of the uterus and heavy lochia
options.B: Long-term fecal incontinence and painful intercourse
options.C: Chronic pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility
options.D: Permanent loss of bladder control and urine leakage

explanation: If sphincter damage isn't caught and repaired properly, it can lead to lifelong struggles with bowel control and painful sex.

question: What happens when a nurse washes their hands properly between patients?

options.A: It permanently cures the patient of chronic illnesses
options.B: It creates a new portal of entry for beneficial flora
options.C: It breaks the mode of transmission link in the chain
options.D: It destroys the genetic material of the reservoir host

explanation: Handwashing removes or kills germs, stopping them from traveling from one person to another. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h2)

question: How does health care economics actually affect you as a nurse on the ward?

options.A: It removes all financial stress from the hospital
options.B: It stops nurses from ever using advanced equipment
options.C: It dictates how staff manage limited supplies and time
options.D: It determines the exact salary of every patient

explanation: Exactly! Every day on the ward, you live economics when juggling limited shifts, gloves, and medication supplies to give the best care possible.

question: How can nurses directly help reduce the problem of under-prescription?

options.A: By replacing missing physician orders with over-the-counter remedies
options.B: By advocating for evidence-based treatments during multidisciplinary rounds
options.C: By writing independent prescriptions for specialized cardiac drugs
options.D: By discharging patients early when medications are unavailable

explanation: You got it! Because nurses spend the most time with patients, they are in the best position to spot missing therapies and speak up during team meetings.

question: What is one of the biggest challenges facing local disaster agencies in Nigeria?

options.A: Chronic underfunding and a lack of modern rescue equipment
options.B: An excessive surplus of advanced medical helicopters
options.C: Strict adherence to international space agency guidelines
options.D: Too many trained volunteers refusing to work

explanation: That's right. Many local agencies struggle simply because tight budgets make it hard to buy modern gear and keep emergency vehicles running.

question: What is the main goal of pharmacovigilance in healthcare?

options.A: Marketing new pharmaceutical products to regional hospitals
options.B: Detecting, assessing, and preventing adverse drug effects
options.C: Speeding up the clinical drug trial approval process
options.D: Calculating the financial cost of manufactured medications

explanation: Pharmacovigilance is the ongoing safety monitoring process designed to catch and prevent drug-related harm. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T2#GNS215_U5_T2_h8)

question: How many total degrees are in a full circle used for a pie chart?

options.A: 360 degrees
options.B: 100 degrees
options.C: 180 degrees
options.D: 90 degrees

explanation: Spot on! A full circle is always 360 degrees all the way round.

question: What fluid mainly fills the hollow chambers (ventricles) inside the brain?

options.A: Venous whole blood
options.B: Cerebrospinal fluid
options.C: Lymphatic interstitial fluid
options.D: Extracellular matrix

explanation: Great job! The brain ventricles are special hollow spaces that continuously make and store cerebrospinal fluid to keep the brain cushioned and nourished.

question: Your patient looks really nervous before you check their tummy (abdomen). What should you do first?

options.A: Scold the patient for being uncooperative
options.B: Skip the abdominal examination entirely
options.C: Proceed immediately without speaking to avoid wasting time
options.D: Explain the steps of the procedure and encourage relaxation

explanation: Kindness goes a long way! Explaining what you're about to do calms their nerves, which actually relaxes their belly muscles so you can get much more accurate exam results.

question: Who usually develops tactical objectives in a healthcare organization?

options.A: Patients recovering in the inpatient wards
options.B: Middle managers like nurse managers and department heads
options.C: Maintenance staff fixing equipment in the basement
options.D: The top chief executive officer working alone

explanation: Department heads and nurse managers take broad executive goals and turn them into departmental action plans. [learn more](GST321_U2_T3#GST321_U2_T3_h4)

question: How do drugs like sildenafil (Viagra) help treat erectile dysfunction?

options.A: They act as direct agonists on alpha-1 adrenergic receptors
options.B: They increase sympathetic tone to close the venous channels
options.C: They directly stimulate the release of acetylcholine from nerve endings
options.D: They block phosphodiesterase type 5 to preserve cGMP levels

explanation: Brilliant! By blocking the enzyme that breaks down cGMP, these drugs help keep the muscles relaxed and blood flowing smoothly.

question: How do membrane filters clean liquid solutions of microorganisms?

options.A: By releasing chemical gases that dissolve the cell walls
options.B: By using high heat to boil away all bacterial contamination
options.C: By physically trapping microbes based on microscopic pore size
options.D: By emitting gamma radiation to destroy microbial DNA

explanation: Think of a membrane filter like a tiny microscopic sieve. The holes are so small that bacteria just get caught right on top!

question: What is the main difference between geriatrics and gerontology?

options.A: The historical study of ancient human populations
options.B: The medical treatment of diseases in older adults
options.C: The financial planning of retired workers
options.D: The social structures of aging communities

explanation: You've got this! Geriatrics focuses specifically on medical care and treating illnesses in older people, while gerontology is the broader study of the overall aging process.

question: Which agency in Nigeria is officially in charge of tracking drug safety and pharmacovigilance?

options.A: NAFDAC
options.B: FMOH
options.C: NMNC
options.D: NMA

explanation: Correct! NAFDAC regulates food and drugs in Nigeria and runs the National Pharmacovigilance Centre to keep watch on drug safety.

question: Where does blood go immediately after leaving the right side of the newborn's heart?

options.A: To the lungs
options.B: To the liver
options.C: To the placenta
options.D: To the brain

explanation: The right side of the heart pumps deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary arteries directly to the lungs for oxygen. [learn more](GNS121_U6_T9#GNS121_U6_T9_h6)

question: Which specialized skin cells make the pigment melanin?

options.A: Melanocytes
options.B: Fibroblasts
options.C: Langerhans cells
options.D: Keratinocytes

explanation: Correct! Melanocytes are the clever cells in our lower epidermis that produce melanin. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h5)

question: What does interdependence mean within a healthcare system?

options.A: Every hospital department operates completely on its own
options.B: A change or delay in one part directly affects other parts
options.C: Financial profit is shared equally among all workers
options.D: Only doctors have an impact on overall patient recovery

explanation: Interdependence means elements rely on each other, so a failure or slowdown in one area ripples through the rest of the system. [learn more](GST319_U2_T6#GST319_U2_T6_h3)

question: What is the main goal of Targeted Temperature Management (TTM) after cardiac arrest?

options.A: To melt any blood clots inside the coronary arteries
options.B: To stimulate the heart to beat faster on its own
options.C: To protect the brain from injury by controlling body temperature
options.D: To help the kidneys filter out emergency medications

explanation: Cooling the body helps reduce brain swelling and metabolic demand after oxygen deprivation. [learn more](GNS315_U4_T4#GNS315_U4_T4_h7)

question: How can you, as a nurse, help a patient build resilience during a long, hard recovery?

options.A: By isolating them from family members to encourage independence
options.B: By doing every single daily task for them to avoid stress
options.C: By helping them focus on controllable factors and celebrating small victories
options.D: By telling them to ignore all negative feelings completely

explanation: Big recoveries are overwhelming. Breaking goals down into small wins helps patients feel capable and gives them the strength to keep going.

question: What is the main hazard of leaving heavy oxygen cylinders unmounted inside an ambulance?

options.A: They make the ambulance engine consume more diesel fuel
options.B: They will automatically run out of medical oxygen faster
options.C: They can become dangerous projectiles during sudden braking
options.D: They interfere with the vehicle's internal electrical system

explanation: Sudden stops create massive forward momentum, turning loose heavy items into severe safety hazards for the crew and patient. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T9#GNS315_U3_T9_h2)

question: Why do multiple humanitarian agencies need to work together during a major refugee crisis?

options.A: International agencies prefer to work in complete isolation from locals.
options.B: Government health ministries are legally banned from helping refugees.
options.C: It eliminates the need for any professional nursing staff on site.
options.D: No single organization has all the resources required to meet complex needs.

explanation: Crises are massive! Providing shelter, clean water, food, and healthcare all at once requires teamwork and pooled resources from many different organizations.

question: Why might an elderly patient with slow kidneys need a smaller drug dose?

options.A: Cellular receptors disappear entirely from target tissues
options.B: Excretion is slower, increasing the risk of drug accumulation and toxicity
options.C: Absorption in the stomach increases rapidly with advanced age
options.D: Liver metabolism stops working completely after age sixty

explanation: When kidneys clear drugs more slowly, the medicine hangs around longer. Adjusting doses prevents accidental overload. Makes sense, right?

question: During a hospital food poisoning investigation, who makes the best control group?

options.A: Healthy volunteers recruited from a local university far away from the hospital
options.B: Patients admitted to the same hospital who did not eat the contaminated food and have no gastrointestinal illness
options.C: Patients who have recovered from the same food poisoning outbreak
options.D: Doctors and nurses who worked in the hospital kitchen

explanation: Great choice! Good controls come from the same environment and background population, but are thankfully free of the illness.

question: What standard assessment tool do nurses use to monitor patients for early signs of tardive dyskinesia?

options.A: APGAR scoring system
options.B: Braden Scale for Pressure Ulcers
options.C: AIMS (Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale)
options.D: Glasgow Coma Scale

explanation: We use the AIMS scale during regular check-ups to score any involuntary twitching or movements so we catch tardive dyskinesia early.

question: What does 'cross-contamination' mean in a kitchen setting?

options.A: The transfer of harmful pathogens from one surface or food to another
options.B: The chemical reaction that occurs when mixing two different spices
options.C: The freezing of fresh vegetables at incorrect freezer temperatures
options.D: The natural spoilage of food caused by exposure to direct sunlight

explanation: Spot on! Cross-contamination happens when germs travel from a dirty source (like raw meat) over to safe food (like a fresh salad).

question: What normally kicks off a 'secondary' wave of movement (peristalsis) in the oesophagus?

options.A: Distension of the oesophageal wall by a trapped food bolus
options.B: Relaxation of the lower sphincter caused by stomach acid
options.C: Sympathetic stimulation from the thoracic chain ganglia
options.D: Direct voluntary signals sent from the cerebral cortex

explanation: Spot on! If a piece of food gets stuck or stretches the wall, local nerves trigger a secondary squeeze to clear out whatever the first wave left behind.

question: A village thinks their stream water is fine, but lab tests show it is full of harmful bacteria. The nurse steps in to treat the water. What kind of need is this?

options.A: Normative need
options.B: Expressed need
options.C: Comparative need
options.D: Felt need

explanation: Even though the villagers didn't complain, professional testing uncovered the hidden danger. That expert-defined standard makes it a normative need!

question: Why should families pick a specific meeting place outside their home when planning for emergencies?

options.A: To ensure everyone can reunite safely if separated during an evacuation
options.B: To provide a storage space for heavy rescue tools
options.C: To serve as a temporary community clinic
options.D: To give neighbors a place to park their vehicles

explanation: Brilliant! Having a pre-arranged meeting spot saves precious time and stops panic if family members get separated during a sudden crisis.

question: What is a major sign of compartment syndrome that sets it apart from normal fracture pain?

options.A: Severe pain that is not relieved by prescribed opioid pain medication
options.B: Sharp pain that completely disappears after taking deep breaths
options.C: Mild aching pain that occurs only when the patient stands up
options.D: Gradual itching underneath the cast as the bone begins to heal

explanation: When strong pain meds don't touch the pain at all, think compartment syndrome! It means dangerous pressure is building up inside the muscle.

question: What common economic challenge often forces families to rely heavily on cheap, refined carbohydrate meals?

options.A: A total lack of agricultural land for farming throughout the entire country
options.B: Financial poverty that makes fresh vegetables and lean proteins expensive
options.C: Universal free distribution of processed foods at primary healthcare centres
options.D: Strict government bans on importing nutritious food items into local markets

explanation: You've got it. Economic reality plays a huge role in health. When fresh protein and veggies are pricey, families naturally turn to cheaper, filling carbs.

question: What is the main goal of studying 'human factors' in nursing?

options.A: Increasing the number of night shifts a nurse can work
options.B: Punishing nurses who make mistakes during medication rounds
options.C: Reducing the salary costs of hospital administrative staff
options.D: Matching clinical work systems to human strengths and limits

question: How does cultural stigma affect the two-way referral process?

options.A: It ensures that primary health clinics receive adequate funding from local chiefs
options.B: It delays initial professional help-seeking, often bringing clients to the hospital only in severe crises
options.C: It makes downward referral unnecessary because clients recover faster at home
options.D: It encourages families to maintain smooth communication with tertiary psychiatrists

explanation: Because of stigma, families often try other options first. By the time they reach the hospital, the illness has usually progressed to a crisis.

question: What does professional autonomy mean for a modern clinical nurse?

options.A: Working completely isolated from doctors and laboratory scientists
options.B: Making independent, accountable clinical decisions within one's scope of practice
options.C: Refusing to follow hospital administrative policies or protocols
options.D: Prescribing major pharmaceutical drugs without medical supervision

explanation: Exactly! Autonomy means having the confidence and professional right to make sound clinical choices within your training limits.

question: You are preparing a postpartum mother with severe bleeding for emergency transfer. What is an essential step?

options.A: Instructing her to walk to the ambulance to improve circulation
options.B: Securing an intravenous (IV) line and starting fluid resuscitation
options.C: Administering strong oral pain relievers
options.D: Waiting for blood test results before allowing her to leave

explanation: Getting an IV line running replaces lost fluids and holds her blood pressure steady during the bumpy ride to the hospital.

question: Why do nurses do a baseline neurologic assessment when a patient is first admitted?

options.A: To determine the exact cost of hospital care
options.B: To replace the need for diagnostic imaging scans
options.C: To cure underlying nerve cell damage
options.D: To detect any changes in patient status over time

explanation: Think of a baseline as your starting snapshot! It gives you a reference point so if the patient's condition changes later, you can spot it right away.

question: What is the safest thing to do with a used needle and syringe right after an injection?

options.A: Drop it directly into a rigid safety box without recapping
options.B: Recap the needle carefully using both hands to protect others

question: When there's no institutional funding for a nursing study, what do nurses often end up doing?

options.A: Abandon clinical duties to work in foreign labs
options.B: Rely entirely on free pharmaceutical samples
options.C: Close down the hospital ward permanently
options.D: Sponsor their own studies out of pocket

question: What is a common traditional barrier to assertiveness in hospitals?

options.A: Excessive training on communication skills
options.B: A complete lack of clinical handovers
options.C: Too many patient safety checklists
options.D: Strict medical hierarchy and fear of punishment

question: What do we call the social, economic, and environmental factors that shape people's health?

options.A: Determinants of health

options.C: Clinical diagnoses
options.D: Phenomenological traits

question: What is endometritis?

options.A: A blood clot inside the deep veins of the leg

question: What is the term for a patient's right to make independent decisions about their own medical treatment?

options.A: Beneficence
options.B: Negligence
options.C: Autonomy
options.D: Malpractice

question: Why might a patient with an enlarged heart (specifically an enlarged left atrium) find it hard to swallow?

options.A: The atrium presses directly against the anterior wall of the adjacent oesophagus.

question: What is a common misconception about herbal and complementary medications?

options.A: They can only be bought with a doctor's prescription
options.B: They are chemically identical to synthetic antibiotics
options.C: They never interact with standard hospital drugs
options.D: They are completely harmless because they are natural

question: What simple comfort measure can a nurse suggest for a patient dealing with dry mouth from these drugs?

options.A: Take small sips of water often or suck on sugarless sweets
options.B: Stop drinking all fluids for the rest of the day
options.C: Take your medication right before doing heavy exercise
options.D: Rinse your mouth with strong salt water every single hour

explanation: Brilliant nursing care! Frequent sips of water or sugarless candy keep those mucous membranes nice and comfortable without messing with their blood sugar.

question: A nurse puts on gloves before emptying a patient's urine bag. Which part of the chain of infection is the nurse blocking?

options.A: Reservoir

options.D: Susceptible host

question: Which hormone do the kidneys produce to tell the bone marrow to make red blood cells?

options.A: Thrombopoietin
options.B: Erythropoietin
options.C: Calcitonin
options.D: Melatonin

question: Why is studying insects (entomology) so important for nurses and healthcare workers?

options.A: It helps track how insects spread diseases to humans
options.B: It allows clinicians to classify bacterial strains accurately

options.D: It teaches nurses how to manufacture chemical insecticides

question: A patient scheduled for parole review keeps refusing meds and denies being sick. What should the team do first?

options.A: Approve the release immediately to encourage independence.

question: What is the primary function of a computer?

options.A: Manipulating and processing data

question: Which muscle group makes up the main bulk of the pelvic floor?

options.A: Levator ani

question: Why are sympathetic preganglionic fibers usually shorter than the postganglionic fibers?

options.C: Because they release hormones directly into the bloodstream

question: Why is checking the damage so important after a disaster occurs?

options.C: It guarantees that no future disasters will ever occur in that zone
options.D: It helps agencies quantify losses and plan effective recovery efforts

question: What does the term 'homebound' usually mean for home health care eligibility?

options.A: The patient can run outside and travel without assistance

options.C: Leaving the home requires a major and taxing effort
options.D: The patient refuses to ever see a doctor in a clinic

question: Who are typical members of an interdisciplinary community health team?

options.A: Environmental health officers, social workers, and nurses

question: What is a common misconception regarding family planning services in many communities?

options.A: It is only meant for couples with no children
options.B: It is exclusively a female responsibility
options.C: It is completely free at all hospitals
options.D: It is dangerous for men to discuss it

question: Why should community health nurses know about laws protecting women and children?

options.A: So nurses can personally prosecute abusive husbands in a court of law
options.B: So they can guide vulnerable patients to proper legal aid and social welfare services
options.C: So they can rewrite traditional community inheritance customs themselves

question: Why might a professional athlete be wrongly classified as overweight on a standard BMI chart?

options.A: Their bones are much denser than average
options.B: Their high daily water intake changes the scale

question: What is the biggest benefit of working hand-in-hand with local leaders during health campaigns?

options.A: They diagnose complex medical conditions in clinics

options.C: They help dispel cultural myths and reduce resistance
options.D: They replace the need for public health education entirely

question: In many Nigerian homes, what hazardous substance is most commonly swallowed by young children by accident because it was stored in an empty soft drink bottle?

options.A: Kerosene
options.B: Dry fertilizer
options.C: Carbon monoxide

question: What is one exciting benefit expected from future voice-activated documentation tools?

options.A: Allowing nurses to speak clinical notes while performing procedures

question: Which of these is a clear example of an unsafe injection habit?

question: Why does the itching from a scabies infestation usually feel way worse at night?

options.C: Dry night air increases surface skin cracking

question: How can Nigeria best achieve long-term financial sustainability for its health care system?

question: Which wastewater treatment stage uses helpful oxygen-loving bacteria to break down organic waste?

question: Why is hiding medical mistakes a bad idea in nursing?

options.D: Generalized physical fatigue

options.B: It completely eliminates the need for nursing monitoring

question: Why should newly hired nurses be introduced to the hospital's cultural values during orientation?

question: Why is proper cleaning and drying of nebulizer equipment so critical for patient safety?

options.C: To replace electrolytes lost through morning sickness
options.D: To cure pre-existing chronic bone infections

explanation: Pregnancy causes a major increase in blood volume and requires extra nutrients to support the developing fetus and placenta. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h3)

question: How would you explain 'psychological resilience' in everyday clinical practice?

options.A: The ability to completely avoid all stressful events in life
options.B: A permanent immunity to developing any form of anxiety or sadness
options.C: The capacity to recover and adapt when facing major life hardships
options.D: A physical condition where the brain ignores emotional pain entirely

explanation: Spot on! Resilience isn't about dodging stress—it's about bending without breaking and bouncing back when life knocks you down.

question: Why is it smart to check a menu for a nice mix of colors, textures, and flavors?

options.A: It guarantees that the food will require zero cooking preparation time
options.B: It stimulates appetite and makes the meal more enjoyable to eat
options.C: It prevents the kitchen staff from having to wash dishes afterwards
options.D: It ensures that every food item tastes exactly the same

explanation: Nobody wants a boring, pale plate! Colorful, well-textured food makes patients actually want to eat.

question: Why is checking skin elasticity (turgor) alone not a reliable way to check for dehydration in an older adult?

options.A: Older adults always refuse to let nurses pinch their hands or arms.
options.B: Aging skin naturally loses elasticity, making it look dehydrated even when it is normal.
options.C: Skin turgor only measures protein levels, not the body's water content.
options.D: Older adults produce too much natural sweat to measure skin fluid accurately.

explanation: Spot on! Older skin naturally loses its bounce, so it can look 'tented' even when the person is well-hydrated.

question: How do anticholinergic drugs help stop the airways from narrowing?

options.A: By blocking acetylcholine from attaching to muscarinic receptors
options.B: By replacing lost calcium ions in the muscle tissue
options.C: By destroying the enzymes that break down cAMP
options.D: By stimulating the sympathetic nervous system directly

explanation: Acetylcholine is a chemical that normally tells airways to squeeze shut. Anticholinergics block it from doing its job, keeping your airways nice and open.

question: What makes intravenous therapy risky regarding how fast drugs act?

options.A: The slow onset of therapeutic effects
options.B: Unpredictable absorption from the gut
options.C: Total immunity to local tissue irritation
options.D: The rapid irreversibility of drug action

explanation: You're doing great! Once a medicine goes straight into the vein, you cannot take it back out. That's why we always double-check our doses—reactions happen fast and are harder to reverse than oral pills.

question: What does emotional health really mean for a person?

options.A: Having a high intelligence quotient
options.B: A dynamic state of coping with life and realizing one's potential
options.C: The total absence of any stressful life events
options.D: Always feeling happy and joyful throughout the day

explanation: Emotional health isn't about being happy 24/7 or having zero stress. It's about balance, bouncing back from normal life challenges, and functioning well!

question: Which factor strongly contributes to cholera outbreaks during the rainy season in our communities?

options.A: Lower ambient temperatures at night
options.B: Dry winds blowing dust into houses
options.C: Contamination of drinking water sources
options.D: Increased population migration to cities

explanation: Spot on! Heavy rains easily wash surface waste into local water sources, which is how waterborne infections like cholera spread so quickly.

question: Why do animal hookworm larvae cause wandering red lines on human skin instead of a deeper infection?

options.A: Because humans are accidental dead-end hosts where the larvae cannot complete their life cycle
options.B: Because topical soaps paralyze the nervous system of the parasites immediately
options.C: Because human white blood cells instantly freeze the larvae in place under the skin
options.D: Because the larvae lack the physical strength to bite through muscle fascia

explanation: Since humans aren't their normal hosts, the larvae get confused and wander aimlessly in the top layers of the skin. Makes sense when you picture it!

question: Why is couples counseling often recommended when treating sexual dysfunction?

options.A: Because sexual problems usually impact both partners in the relationship
options.B: To legally bind partners to follow the treatment plan
options.C: Because individual therapy is strictly illegal for sexual issues
options.D: To prove which partner is at fault for the problem

explanation: Intimacy is shared between two people. Involving both partners encourages teamwork and open communication, which speeds up healing.

question: A patient takes too much of an opioid pain medication and their breathing drops to just 4 breaths per minute. Why does this happen?

options.A: Cerebral cortex voluntarily suppressing the urge to breathe
options.B: Peripheral muscles failing to respond to normal nerve signals
options.C: Medullary respiratory centres suppressed by circulating drug molecules
options.D: Carotid baroreceptors shutting off blood flow to the lungs

explanation: Opioids can bind to the brainstem and quiet down the breathing center so much that it forgets to signal the body to breathe at a normal rate.

question: What is the primary focus of accident prevention in nursing care?

options.A: Strict bedrest enforcement
options.B: Expensive home renovations
options.C: Proactive risk identification
options.D: Punishing careless behaviors

explanation: Nurses focus heavily on finding and fixing hazards before an actual injury happens to the patient. [learn more](GNS324_U6_T4#GNS324_U6_T4_h1)

question: What is the main goal when medical help arrives immediately after a disaster?

options.A: To minimize death and illness
options.B: To train local volunteers
options.C: To rebuild damaged hospitals
options.D: To document insurance claims

explanation: You've got this! When disaster strikes, the immediate focus is always on saving lives and stopping severe illness through quick medical action.

question: Why do lecturers love using concept maps and breaking long topics into smaller pieces?

options.A: To replace traditional textbook reading with digital games
options.B: To punish students who do not complete their homework
options.C: To eliminate the need for any practical clinical rotations
options.D: To prevent working memory from experiencing cognitive overload

explanation: Our brains can only juggle so much at once! Breaking info down into "chunks" keeps us from feeling overwhelmed so we can actually understand and remember it.

question: Which of these sits at the very top of the healthcare policy framework?

options.A: Ward shift handover notes
options.B: National laws and legislative acts
options.C: Hospital-wide administrative bylaws
options.D: Individual departmental protocols

explanation: Always remember: external national laws and acts overrule every internal hospital rule and departmental guideline.

question: Why does a severe shortage of nursing staff increase medication errors in a hospital ward?

options.A: Nurses forget how to read prescriptions over time
options.B: Pharmacies stop supplying drugs to overworked units
options.C: Patients refuse to take their drugs unless a doctor gives them
options.D: Rushed nurses juggling too many patients are more likely to miss critical safety steps

explanation: Overworked and exhausted nurses dealing with excessive workloads face a much higher risk of making mistakes. [learn more](GST322_U4_T2#GST322_U4_T2_h6)

question: What is the best first step when a nurse finds out a patient believes a harmful food myth?

options.A: Listen openly to understand their reasoning without immediate judgment
options.B: Laugh at the idea to show how ridiculous the myth is
options.C: Hand them a lengthy research textbook to read
options.D: Refuse to treat the patient until they change their diet

explanation: Empathy and active listening build instant trust. When patients feel heard, they are much more open to your nursing guidance!

question: During a vasectomy, which main tube is cut or blocked to stop sperm from leaving?

options.A: The vas deferens
options.B: The seminal vesicles
options.C: The seminiferous tubules
options.D: The epididymis

explanation: You got this! The vas deferens is the muscular tube that carries sperm from the testes, making it the exact target for this procedure.

question: What is the most common cause of heavy bleeding right after childbirth (primary PPH)?

options.A: Retained surgical gauze
options.B: Uterine atony
options.C: Coagulation disorders
options.D: Cervical laceration

explanation: Spot on! Uterine atony happens when the uterine muscles are too tired to clamp down after delivery. Recognizing this helps you save mothers every day!

question: Which requirement must be met before skilled home health nursing care can officially start?

options.A: The family must purchase a private hospital bed
options.B: The patient must win a local community award
options.C: A licensed physician must order the care
options.D: The nurse must live with the patient full-time

explanation: Home health services require a formal medical order from a doctor just like any other prescription or therapy. [learn more](GNS324_U1_T8#GNS324_U1_T8_h8)

question: Why does a strict blame culture hurt patient safety over time?

options.A: It makes staff hide mistakes and close calls out of fear
options.B: It places too much financial burden on the hospital administration
options.C: It makes nurses calculate medications by hand more often
options.D: It stops nurses from getting proper clinical certifications

explanation: When punishment is guaranteed, nurses stay quiet. We need open communication to fix dangerous processes together!

question: A study compares lung cancer patients with healthy people, looking backward at their past smoking habits. What kind of study is this?

options.A: Prospective cohort study
options.B: Qualitative ethnography
options.C: Case-control study
options.D: Randomized controlled trial

explanation: Think of a case-control study as looking in the rearview mirror. You start with the 'cases' (people who have the condition) and look backward at their past exposures compared to healthy controls.

question: What is a major public health challenge linked to teenage pregnancies?

options.A: Immediate onset of chronic hypertension
options.B: Permanent cessation of natural bone growth
options.C: Decreased overall societal life expectancy
options.D: Increased maternal morbidity and mortality

explanation: Complications from early childbirth and unsafe procedures are major reasons young mothers face serious health risks. You've got this!

question: Why is disease surveillance often called an early warning system?

options.A: It predicts exact weather conditions for disease outbreaks.
options.B: It helps health workers spot unusual patterns before an epidemic grows.
options.C: It automatically cures patients before they visit the hospital.
options.D: It replaces the need for laboratory testing entirely.

explanation: Spotting rising cases early lets health workers jump in and take action before a tiny bump turns into a full-blown outbreak!

question: Why would a patient who took a severe drug overdose be put on a mechanical ventilator?

options.A: Reversal of central nervous system toxicity
options.B: Immediate elimination of the drug from the lungs
options.C: Airway protection and respiratory support
options.D: Prevention of future drug dependency

explanation: When someone is deeply unconscious from an overdose, their body forgets to protect its own airway. The ventilator keeps them breathing safely and stops any spit or vomit from entering their lungs.

question: What procurement practice helps health authorities buy essential medicines at a much lower cost?

options.A: Bulk purchasing using generic non-proprietary names
options.B: Ordering exclusively through expensive luxury suppliers
options.C: Importing only patented brand-name formulations
options.D: Buying small batches from local retail pharmacies daily

explanation: Great job! Buying large quantities of generics lets health systems take advantage of bulk discounts.

question: In a good data story, what is the second step after setting the scene?

options.A: Offering a detailed financial budget for the next year
options.B: Introducing the conflict by revealing the problem in the data
options.C: Setting the scene by describing normal unit operations
options.D: Listing every single nurse who worked on the night shift

explanation: You nailed it! Once you show how things normally work, you bring in the main problem—like a spike in patient infections or falls.

question: What is a major money-related barrier for women in patriarchal communities trying to get healthcare?

options.A: An excessive number of female-only medical clinics
options.B: Too many job opportunities outside the home
options.C: Universal health insurance coverage for men only
options.D: Lack of independent income and financial control

explanation: When women don't control their own money, it becomes very hard to pay for transport to the clinic or buy needed medicines on their own.

question: Why do teenagers sometimes make impulsive choices or take big risks?

options.A: The nervous system completely stops communicating during teen years
options.B: The emotional brain matures faster than the planning center of the brain
options.C: The body produces too much calcium during early puberty growth spurts
options.D: Teenagers lose their long-term memory capacity temporarily

explanation: Exactly! Because the emotional part of the brain develops quicker than the logical planning part, teens often feel strong urges before they fully weigh the consequences.

question: What is the big difference between bactericidal and bacteriostatic drugs?

options.A: Bactericidal agents require acidic pH, while bacteriostatic agents need alkaline pH
options.B: Bacteriostatic drugs work only in the lungs, while bactericidal drugs work everywhere
options.C: Bactericidal drugs kill bacteria, whereas bacteriostatic drugs stop their growth
options.D: Bacteriostatic drugs destroy human cells, but bactericidal drugs protect them

explanation: Easy to remember: Bacterici-DAL drugs outright KILL the bacteria, while bacteriostatic drugs just press 'pause' on their growth and let your immune system finish the job!

question: What makes a host a 'dead-end host' during an infection?

options.A: The host destroys the infectious agent completely upon first contact
options.B: The host harbors the adult parasite for many years without harm
options.C: The host cannot pass the infection on to other susceptible individuals
options.D: The host dies immediately before any symptoms can manifest

explanation: Think of it as a dead-end street. The pathogen gets stuck inside this host and cannot travel any further to infect other people.

question: How does community stigma negatively affect disease surveillance data?

options.A: It speeds up the transmission of weekly health reports to the capital.
options.B: It causes people to hide sick family members and avoid visiting clinics.
options.C: It automatically increases the national budget allocation for health.
options.D: It forces laboratories to buy more expensive testing equipment.

explanation: When people are scared of being judged or isolated, they hide their illnesses at home, leading to missing cases and inaccurate health stats.

question: What is the main job of our respiratory system?

options.A: Producing red blood cells
options.B: Bringing in oxygen and removing carbon dioxide
options.C: Regulating body temperature
options.D: Filtering bacteria out of the bloodstream

explanation: Spot on! The lungs trade gases with every breath we take—bringing in fresh oxygen our body loves and blowing out waste carbon dioxide.

question: What do we call the medical measurement of the inside of a woman's pelvis to check if she can deliver vaginally?

options.A: Hysteroscopy
options.B: Amniocentesis
options.C: Episiotomy
options.D: Pelvimetry

explanation: You've got this! Pelvimetry is just measuring the birth canal dimensions to make sure everything can fit safely.

question: What kind of mistake happens when a busy nurse accidentally documents care in someone else's chart?

options.A: Data omission
options.B: Transcription error
options.C: Duplicate entry
options.D: Wrong-patient charting

explanation: Entering notes into the wrong file is a risky mix-up that usually happens when things get too rushed on the ward.

question: What is the common name for onchocerciasis?

options.A: Sleeping sickness
options.B: River blindness
options.C: Elephantiasis
options.D: Swamp fever

explanation: Onchocerciasis is widely known as river blindness because the blackfly vectors breed near fast-flowing rivers where transmission is highest. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T7#GNS214_U1_T7_h1)

question: If a delay in the hospital pharmacy slows down when a ward nurse can teach a patient about their discharge drugs, what does this show?

options.A: Traditional epistemological habit
options.B: Appreciation of a system
options.C: Individual cognitive bias
options.D: Understanding clinical variation

explanation: Spot on! This shows how one part of the hospital (pharmacy) directly links to and affects another part (the ward nurse's workflow).

question: Why isn't the CA-125 blood test used as a general screening tool for healthy women?

options.A: It only detects cancer after it has already spread to the brain
options.B: It requires a painful surgical biopsy before the blood sample is drawn
options.C: It can be elevated by non-cancerous conditions like endometriosis or menstruation
options.D: The cost of the test is too high for public healthcare systems

explanation: You nailed it. Normal things like your period or harmless cysts can also make CA-125 levels rise, leading to false alarms.

question: Why do nurses convert raw tally numbers into percentages and rates when analyzing data?

options.A: To make the final report look more complicated to read
options.B: To eliminate the need to collect any information from households
options.C: To make the health findings easier to interpret and compare
options.D: To prevent community members from understanding the results

explanation: Spot on! Percentages and rates give meaning to raw numbers, helping us clearly see the proportion of people affected by an issue.

question: When is a simple hand wash with ordinary soap and water best to use?

options.A: After handling visibly soiled items or using the restroom
options.B: Immediately before inserting a central venous catheter
options.C: Before assisting in major open-heart surgery
options.D: When hands are completely dry and free of visible dirt

explanation: When your hands are visibly dirty or messy, plain soap and water are your best friends for a physical clean-up.

question: A patient says, 'My life is completely useless.' The nurse replies, 'You feel that your life has no meaning right now?' What communication skill is this?

options.A: Defending an institutional rule
options.B: Giving premature advice
options.C: Changing the conversation subject
options.D: Reflecting the patient's statement

explanation: Brilliant! Reflecting means repeating or paraphrasing the patient's feelings back to them. It shows you are actively listening and encourages them to open up more.

question: Why does high national debt servicing negatively affect public health budgets?

options.A: It directly increases the number of patients seeking private insurance
options.B: It forces international health organizations to withdraw all nursing staff
options.C: It automatically lowers the market price of essential pharmaceutical drugs
options.D: It drains government revenue that could otherwise be allocated to social sectors like health

explanation: When a huge chunk of national income goes to paying off debts, less money is left in the purse for hospitals, schools, and health programs.

question: How do upfront hospital user fees usually affect patients with little income?

options.A: They are given free medications upon arrival
options.B: They are automatically transferred to private suites
options.C: They receive faster treatment than wealthy patients
options.D: They delay seeking care until their condition worsens

explanation: Exactly right. Worrying about money often causes vulnerable patients to stay home until a simple illness turns into a major emergency.

question: Why are electronic monitors so helpful when looking after unstable patients?

options.A: They make writing shift notes completely unnecessary
options.B: They catch small downward trends before a full crisis hits
options.C: They prevent any sudden changes from ever occurring
options.D: They stop false alarms from ever happening

explanation: Continuous tracking shows tiny shifts in a patient's stability long before a normal manual check would pick them up. Great clinical thinking!

question: What is the main drawback of the immune response triggered by T-independent antigens?

options.A: They completely prevent any immediate white blood cell activation
options.B: They destroy healthy host tissues alongside invading pathogens
options.C: They fail to create strong long-term immunological memory
options.D: They require months of processing before antibodies appear

explanation: Without T-cells stepping in to help, the body reacts quickly but fails to build long-lasting memory cells for future protection.

question: What is the ultimate goal for many participants in a sheltered workshop?

options.A: Remaining in the workshop facility for their entire lives
options.B: Starting an independent manufacturing business alone
options.C: Becoming full-time nursing instructors in hospitals
options.D: Transitioning into open, competitive employment

explanation: These workshops are meant to be a helpful stepping stone toward regular, independent jobs in the community. Almost done with this set!

question: A patient with pneumonia says their chest hurts sharply every time they take a deep breath. What's the most likely reason?

options.A: Sudden spasms of the chest muscles
options.B: Extra pressure inside the right side of the heart
options.C: Inflamed lung linings rubbing against the chest wall
options.D: Irritation of the main breathing tubes in the throat

explanation: That sharp pain is called pleuritic chest pain. It happens when the inflamed outer lining of the lungs (pleura) rubs against the chest wall with every breath.

question: How did modern safety acts like OSHA change workplace safety?

options.A: Establishing legally enforceable safety standards with power to inspect and fine workplaces
options.B: Banning the use of all heavy machinery in manufacturing and construction
options.C: Requiring all industrial workers to retire by age fifty with full pensions
options.D: Leaving workplace safety entirely up to the voluntary discretion of corporate boards

explanation: OSHA turned workplace safety from a nice idea into a strict legal duty, using inspections and fines to keep workers safe.

question: What is a common drawback of relying solely on negative discipline?

options.A: It encourages nurses to ignore all hospital policies
options.B: It takes too much time to implement
options.C: It always improves long-term clinical skills
options.D: It creates resentment and damages teamwork

explanation: Using fear and harsh penalties makes staff fearful, destroying trust and open communication. [learn more](GST321_U1_T22#GST321_U1_T22_h2)

question: What common operational problem often strains the relationship between Nigerian hospitals and HMOs?

options.A: Delayed payments and capitation disbursements by the HMOs
options.B: Enrollees demanding to work as administrative staff in insurance offices
options.C: Hospitals refusing to admit any patients who have insurance
options.D: The government banning all private health insurance schemes

explanation: When HMOs delay remitting capitation or settling service claims, hospitals struggle financially to provide quality medications and care. [learn more](GST322_U4_T8#GST322_U4_T8_h6)

question: What is the main reason why medication rooms in the ward must always be kept locked?

options.A: To prevent unauthorized access and accidental drug mix-ups
options.B: To make it difficult for doctors to write new prescriptions
options.C: To keep the air conditioning inside the room very cold
options.D: To hide hospital supply costs from incoming student nurses

explanation: Locking the drug room keeps powerful medications safe from unauthorized people and helps keep everything organized for the team.

question: How do extrinsic rewards (like cash bonuses or awards) usually affect nurses over time?

options.A: They work exclusively on administrative staff rather than clinicians
options.B: They permanently alter a nurse's core professional values
options.C: They provide effective short-term drive but may lose impact over time
options.D: They completely eliminate the need for supportive workplace leadership

explanation: External perks are nice, but people eventually get used to them. That's why relying only on bonuses isn't enough for long-term happiness at work.

question: Which of these actions breaks patient confidentiality during a home visit?

options.A: Asking a conscious adult patient before sharing details with family
options.B: Locking your paper notes inside a secure bag while traveling
options.C: Writing your visit notes right after leaving the patient's home
options.D: Gossip about the patient's diagnosis with neighbors outside the house

explanation: Spot on! Patient privacy is sacred. Discussing health details with outsiders like neighbors is a serious breach of professional ethics.

question: What should you do with a used needle right after giving an injection?

options.A: Leave it on the medication trolley for later sorting
options.B: Drop it directly into a puncture-resistant safety box
options.C: Recap it carefully using both hands on the tray
options.D: Break the needle off and throw it in the general bin

explanation: Never recap needles! Dropping them straight into the safety box protects you and your colleagues from accidental needle-stick injuries.

question: An AED has just been brought to the side of an adult patient in cardiac arrest. What is the very first thing the nurse should do with it?

options.A: Press the shock button
options.B: Apply the electrode pads
options.C: Check the battery level
options.D: Turn the AED on

explanation: Turning the device on activates the audio and visual prompts that guide the rest of the rescue steps. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h6)

question: Why should nurses understand the role of informal health providers in Nigeria?

options.A: Orthodox hospitals rely entirely on traditional bone setters for major surgery
options.B: Informal providers are legally mandated to supervise hospital nursing staff
options.C: The government requires all nurses to complete training in traditional medicine
options.D: Many patients consult informal practitioners before or alongside orthodox care

explanation: Spot on! Knowing that many patients see traditional healers first helps us understand their health history and guide them better.

question: Where is the main control center or 'thermostat' for human body temperature located?

options.A: The spinal cord
options.B: The medulla oblongata
options.C: The hypothalamus
options.D: The cerebellum

explanation: Well done! The hypothalamus in the brain acts as our internal thermostat, checking our temperature and making adjustments.

question: Which antenatal practice helps prevent prolonged labour complications in our communities?

options.A: Identifying high-risk women and planning facility delivery
options.B: Relying entirely on home remedies for minor labour pains
options.C: Prescribing bed rest for all pregnant women after twenty weeks
options.D: Discouraging any form of physical activity throughout pregnancy

explanation: Excellent! Good antenatal screening lets us spot potential risks early so mothers can plan to deliver safely where expert help is available.

question: Which symptom during the final months of pregnancy strongly points to placenta previa?

options.A: High fever with foul-smelling amniotic fluid
options.B: Sudden swelling of the feet only
options.C: Painless bright red vaginal bleeding
options.D: Severe painful contractions with a rigid belly

question: Why are children under five especially vulnerable during a community disaster?

options.A: They are at high risk of rapid dehydration and severe malnutrition
options.B: They can easily navigate complex evacuation routes alone
options.C: They always carry emergency financial savings
options.D: They possess stronger immune systems than healthy adults

explanation: You got it! Little ones have delicate fluid balances and need regular care, so they deteriorate fast when food and clean water run out.

question: Why is teamwork among different healthcare professionals so crucial in long-term care?

options.A: Medical doctors require assistance to perform basic personal hygiene
options.B: Residents typically have multiple complex physical, emotional, and social needs
options.C: It ensures that nurses never have to communicate with resident families
options.D: It removes the need for documenting resident care assessments

explanation: Brilliant! Because residents have varied needs, nurses, doctors, dietitians, and therapists must work hand-in-hand to cover all bases.

question: A patient has a severe spinal cord injury needing advanced surgery. Where should they be sent?

options.A: Outpatient clinic
options.B: Community post
options.C: Tertiary level
options.D: Primary level

explanation: Spot on! Complex cases like major spine injuries need specialized tertiary hospitals with advanced equipment and expert surgical teams.

question: How can tele-nursing work best in rural areas with limited resources?

options.A: By requiring patients to buy expensive personal computers before getting help
options.B: By waiting until every village has advanced fibre-optic internet cables installed
options.C: By stopping all physical hospital care and replacing it with mobile apps
options.D: By utilizing simple, accessible tools like basic SMS and solar-powered communication points

explanation: You got it! Success in resource-limited settings depends on using affordable, everyday technology that fits local realities rather than waiting for fancy equipment.

question: Nursing informatics is a blend of three major fields. Which ones are they?

options.A: Biology, chemistry, and clinical medicine
options.B: Pharmacology, anatomy, and health administration
options.C: Nursing science, computer science, and information science
options.D: Psychology, sociology, and data technology

explanation: Spot on! Nursing informatics brings together patient care, computers, and data management to make healthcare smoother and safer for everyone.

question: Which of these actions goes against basic computer safety rules in the ward?

options.A: Sharing your personal computer login password with a fellow nurse
options.B: Using a barcode scanner to verify a patient's medication before administration
options.C: Reporting a lagging computer screen to the hospital IT help desk
options.D: Logging out of the electronic health record system when leaving for lunch

explanation: Never share your password! Whatever is charted under your login account is 100% your professional responsibility.

question: Why do combined oral contraceptive pills carry a risk of blood clots?

options.A: Daily pill swallowing thickens the blood cells directly
options.B: Progestin causes severe dehydration in the body
options.C: Sugar pills trigger an inflammatory immune response
options.D: Estrogen stimulates clotting factors in the liver

explanation: Think of it this way: the estrogen part of the pill encourages the liver to produce more clotting proteins, which can raise the chance of blood clots in some patients.

question: What is the main goal of medical treatment for someone with hyperthyroidism?

options.A: Replacing deficient thyroid hormones with synthetic T4
options.B: Blocking all adrenaline receptors in the central nervous system
options.C: Permanently destroying the thyroid gland using chemical agents
options.D: Restoring a normal metabolic state known as euthyroidism
